# What this report is

One patient, two slides. IB1 is a composite lymph node carrying classic Hodgkin lymphoma
beside follicular lymphoma; RB1 is the follicular lymphoma's recurrence, the same clone with
no Hodgkin component. Every result here is descriptive of that one case. RB1's role
throughout is as the negative control: whatever a readout finds in IB1, it must not find in
RB1 if it is to be read as Hodgkin biology.

The question in all of these steps is the same: **where are the Hodgkin–Reed–Sternberg (HRS)
cells, and can anything on this panel identify them?** The answer changed four times. This
report walks the four readouts in the order they were built, says what each established and
where it stopped, and ends with the proposed pathologist review (section 8) and the analyses a
reviewed set would make possible.

<div class="verdict-mid">
**The short version.** Per-cell HRS markers fail on this panel. A regional chemokine readout
(the hotspots) is Hodgkin-specific but is a density detector that misses most of the brightest
cells. Calling cells individually on CCL17+CCL22 brightness is ~300-fold Hodgkin-specific and
the HRS-compatible transcriptional programme climbs with it. But three independent morphology
readouts of those cells — CD45 context, nuclear size, nuclear paleness — each point *away*
from the cells whose RNA is most HRS-like. The hypothesis that reconciles this is that the
vendor segmentation carves giant cells into fragments, and that is what step 35 tests.
</div>

# Direct HRS markers do not work on this panel (step 10)

HRS cells are defined by protein: CD30 and CD15 positive, CD45 negative, weak PAX5, with
large multilobed nuclei and prominent nucleoli. None of the protein markers is on the slide;
CD30 is on the RNA panel as *TNFRSF8*.

```{r s10}
nobj <- if (!is.null(S10)) S10[metric == "IB1_objects_called", value] else NA
robj <- if (!is.null(S10)) S10[metric == "RB1_objects_called", value] else NA
```

- *TNFRSF8* is too sparse to call a cell on. In IB1 it tops out at **6 counts** per cell with
  **78% of detections being single molecules**, and sequencing depth alone predicts its
  detection at **AUC 0.716** (established in step 10 and carried in the step-13 report; the
  depth AUC turned out to be generic, the same for *IGKC*). A threshold on it selects deep
  cells, not CD30-high cells.
- Step 10's attempt to assemble "HRS objects" from CD30-positive segments called
  **`r nobj`** objects in IB1 and **`r robj`** in RB1, the slide with no Hodgkin component — the
  control did not separate from the case.
- The per-cell leakage problem compounds this: transcripts are displaced toward marker-rich
  neighbours (step 18), and every per-cell flag for a miscalled cell sits at chance.

<div class="verdict-no">
**Closed.** Per-cell HRS/CD30 calling is listed as a closed avenue. Any HRS claim on this
dataset has to come from something other than a marker threshold on a single cell.
</div>

# The chemokine hotspots: a regional readout that works, and its blind spot (steps 11–17)

HRS cells secrete CCL17 (TARC) and CCL22 (MDC); serum TARC is a clinical marker of the disease.
Step 11 replaced the per-cell marker with a regional one: the top 1% of 100 µm bins by pooled
CCL17+CCL22, requiring at least 40 cells per bin.

```{r s16}
hot <- if (!is.null(B16)) B16[samp == "IB1" & bin_region == "cHL_hotspot"] else NULL
```

**What the hotspots established** (steps 11, 16, 17; details in `step16_FL_comparison.html`
and `step17_PD1_PDL1.html`):

- **`r if (!is.null(hot)) hot$bins else 80`** hotspots in IB1 holding
  `r if (!is.null(hot)) fmt(hot$cells, 0) else "4,662"` defect-free cells in
  `r if (!is.null(hot)) hot$fovs else 58` fields of view; **zero** RB1 bins clear the same cut.
- The chemokine field around them is real and Hodgkin-specific: it decays 2.71× from
  100–400 µm to >1,600 µm in IB1 against 1.20× in RB1, with most of the decay spent by
  400–800 µm.
- The hotspots are dendritic-cell rather than macrophage territory (cDC1 1.83×, mature DC
  1.59×, macrophage 0.77×) and carry ligand-side checkpoint elevation (*CD274* OR 1.83,
  *PDCD1LG2* 1.92, *PDCD1* flat).

**Where they stop.** A hotspot is a 100 µm bin, so it is a region, not a cell: it cannot be put
in front of a pathologist, and it cannot be given a nucleus. Worse, pooled bin cp10k is a
*density* detector. A ~58-cell bin carries ~19,000 counts, so one cell with 100 chemokine
counts adds ~52 cp10k — under half the hotspot cut — while two or three moderate cells add
as much.

```{r s28hot}
t28 <- if (!is.null(T28)) T28[samp == "IB1"] else NULL
n50 <- if (!is.null(t28)) t28[tier %in% c("50-99", "100+"), sum(cells)] else NA
in50 <- if (!is.null(t28)) t28[tier %in% c("50-99", "100+"), sum(in_hotspot)] else NA
n100 <- g(t28, tier == "100+", cells); in100 <- g(t28, tier == "100+", in_hotspot)
no100 <- if (!is.null(H28)) H28[n100 == 0, .N] else NA
```

- Of the **`r fmt(n50, 0)`** IB1 cells with ≥ 50 chemokine counts, only
  **`r fmt(in50, 0)` (`r pct(in50 / n50)`)** sit inside a hotspot; of the **`r fmt(n100, 0)`**
  with ≥ 100 counts, `r fmt(in100, 0)` (`r pct(in100 / n100)`).
- **`r no100` of `r if (!is.null(H28)) nrow(H28) else 80`** hotspots contain no cell with ≥ 100
  counts at all. In the median hotspot, cells with ≥ 50 counts supply under half of its
  chemokine.
- Step 11's 50/100/200 µm bin-size sweep kept the same pooled rule at every scale and so never
  tested this.

```{r fig-hot, out.width="60%"}
fig("fig_11_hotspot_myeloid_vs_dc.png")
```

<div class="verdict-mid">
**Kept, with its scope narrowed.** The hotspots remain the tissue-scale Hodgkin readout — the
field extent, its decay and its checkpoint profile stand. They are not an enumeration of the
cells that make the chemokine. A 1 mm view around one hotspot (the first figure of the next
section) shows dozens of isolated bright sources with the three hotspot boxes in the square
holding 10% of its chemokine.
</div>

# Bright cells: the per-cell readout (steps 27–29)

```{r fig-37a, out.width="85%"}
fig("hotspots_miss_most_bright_cells.png")
```

The blind spot on the image: a 1 mm square of IB1 centred on hotspot IB1_55_162, DAPI in
grey with the CCL17+CCL22 molecule density over it (Gaussian σ 8 µm, molecules per 100 µm²,
the same colour clamp as the step-29 review set). The three cyan boxes are the step-11
hotspot bins in the square; the orange arc is the edge of an FL neighbourhood. Most of the
bright sources — the near-white spots — sit outside every box, because a box scores pooled
density over a 100 µm bin and one bright cell is diluted by the ~58 others around it. Note
that this is raw molecule density, not cp10k, so it also rises wherever cells are packed.

```{r fig-37b, out.width="100%"}
fig("IB1_57_161_zoom.png")
```

Zooming in on the seam hotspot in the lower left of that square (IB1_57_161, 200 µm at full
resolution). **A** repeats the DAPI + density view at the 1 mm figure's scale. **B** is the
step-35 panel style: the DNA / CD45 / Membrane composite with every vendor polygon outlined
(warm, with its count, where CCL17+CCL22 ≥ 20; thin orange 10–19; grey otherwise), every
molecule as a dot coloured by transcript (CCL17 green, CCL22 cyan) and the step-29 density rings at 6 / 12 / 24 molecules per 100 µm². This box does hold the
brightest source in its field: of the **`r g(X37, , n_molecules_in_box)`** molecules inside
it, **`r g(X37, , n_in_bright_polygons)` (`r pct(g(X37, , n_in_bright_polygons) / g(X37, , n_molecules_in_box), 0)`)**
sit in `r g(X37, , n_bright_polygons)` polygons with ≥ 20 counts — three of them touching
(90 / 38 / 25, one step-35 composite in the lower right of the box, which the molecule cloud
and the rings draw as a single source) plus a separate 24-count cell. The bin's cp10k then pools that source with the ~40 other cells in the box,
which is why a composite of this size can clear the cut while an isolated bright cell (the
112-count cell at the left edge of the window) cannot: the bin scores density, so it finds
clusters and grouped sources and misses most of the isolated ones.

Dropping the bins and ranking cells by their own CCL17+CCL22 count turned out to be the
specific readout the hotspots were approximating.

## Specificity

```{r s28tier}
t28r <- if (!is.null(T28)) T28[samp == "RB1"] else NULL
r50 <- if (!is.null(t28r)) t28r[tier %in% c("50-99", "100+"), sum(cells)] else NA
r100 <- if (!is.null(t28r)) t28r[tier == "100+", sum(cells)] else 0
tot_i <- if (!is.null(t28)) t28[, sum(cells)] else NA; tot_r <- if (!is.null(t28r)) t28r[, sum(cells)] else NA
tab <- data.table(`CCL17+CCL22 per cell` = c("≥ 50", "≥ 100"),
                  IB1 = c(fmt(n50, 0), fmt(n100, 0)), RB1 = c(fmt(r50, 0), fmt(r100, 0)),
                  `IB1 : RB1 per cell` = c(fmt((n50 / tot_i) / max(r50 / tot_r, 1e-9), 0), if (r100 == 0) "no RB1 cell" else fmt((n100 / tot_i) / (r100 / tot_r), 0)))
kb(tab, caption = sprintf("Bright cells by sample (defect-free matched-tier cells: IB1 %s, RB1 %s).", fmt(tot_i, 0), fmt(tot_r, 0)))
```

Cells with 10–49 counts exist in both samples (activated dendritic cells and macrophages also
make these chemokines); cells with ≥ 50 are essentially confined to the Hodgkin slide.

```{r fig-rank, out.width="75%"}
fig("fig29_chemokine_rank.png")
```

## The programme climbs with brightness, and it is not the dendritic-cell programme

Each gene's excess is observed over expected counts, expected from cells with < 10 chemokine
counts in the same depth decile (depth excluding the chemokine counts themselves), FOV cluster
bootstrap.

```{r s28genes}
tv <- if (!is.null(TV28)) TV28[samp == "IB1" & gene %in% c("BATF3", "IL13", "TNFRSF8", "IRF4", "LTA", "LAMP3", "XCR1", "CD1C", "IDO1", "CCR7", "CD80", "LYZ", "CD68")] else NULL
if (!is.null(tv)) kb(tv[order(-ratio_100_vs_10), .(gene, set, `100+ vs 10-19` = fmt(ratio_100_vs_10), lo = fmt(lo), hi = fmt(hi), q = signif(q, 2))],
                     caption = "Ratio of excess, 100+ tier over 10-19 tier, IB1. HRS-leaning and shared activation genes rise; dendritic-cell lineage genes do not.")
```

```{r fig-excess, out.width="100%"}
fig("fig29_brightness_gene_excess.png")
```

The genes that rise are of two kinds: those HRS cells are known for (*IL13*, *TNFRSF8*/CD30,
*LTA*, *IRF4*) and an activated antigen-presenting programme (*BATF3*, *CD80*, *CD83*, *CD40*,
*CCR7*) that HRS cells and mature dendritic cells share. The genes that would mark a dendritic
cell as such — *LAMP3*, *XCR1*, *CLEC9A*, *CD1C*, *IDO1* — stay flat or fall.

## The HRS-leaning genes sit in the same cells

```{r s28co}
co <- if (!is.null(CO28)) CO28[samp == "IB1" & !grepl("\\[", combo)] else NULL
if (!is.null(co)) kb(co[, .(combo, `O/E` = fmt(oe), lo = fmt(oe_lo), hi = fmt(oe_hi), `null median` = fmt(null_median), `p vs null` = signif(p_null, 2))],
                     caption = "Co-positivity among IB1 source cells (≥ 10 counts): observed over expected under independence within depth × brightness strata, against random detection-matched gene sets.")
```

*IL13*, *BATF3* and *TNFRSF8* co-occur at **`r if (!is.null(co)) fmt(co[combo == "IL13+BATF3+TNFRSF8", oe]) else "1.36"`×** independence — the same
strength as the B-cell and T-cell lineage pairs used as controls — while the activated-DC pair
*CCR7*–*LAMP3* does not co-occur at all. There is no mregDC subpopulation among the sources.

```{r fig-co, out.width="85%"}
fig("fig29_cooccurrence_vs_null.png")
```

<details><summary>Why brightness, not the three genes, is the filter</summary>

```{r s28k3}
k <- if (!is.null(K28)) K28[tier %in% c("10-19", "20-49", "50-99", "100+")] else NULL
if (!is.null(k)) kb(k[, .(samp, tier, n, `≥ 2 of 3` = pct(k2 + k3), `all 3` = pct(k3))], caption = "Share of source cells carrying IL13 / BATF3 / TNFRSF8.")
```

Among ≥ 50 cells the triple is only ~15 cells above independence, and "≥ 2 of 3" is just ~2×
more common in IB1 than in RB1 at matched brightness, so a gene gate would admit cells with no
HRS biology about half the time. Brightness ≥ 50 is ~300× Hodgkin-specific. The genes rank
candidates; they do not call them.
</details>

## Where the bright cells sit

```{r s29fl}
f <- if (!is.null(FL29)) FL29[axis == "d_fl_um" & thr == "n50" & grepl("<=40", band)] else NULL
```

Raw rates look enriched inside the follicular-lymphoma footprint, but FL tissue is deeper and a
count threshold is easier to reach in deep cells. Depth-standardised, the ratio in the footprint
is **`r if (!is.null(f)) sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", fmt(f$adj), fmt(f$adj_lo), fmt(f$adj_hi)) else "1.61 [0.83, 2.40]"`**: bright cells are not excluded from the FL, and
not clearly drawn to it either.

## The review set

Step 29 produced 120 full-resolution ROI images of bright cells in six groups (high, medium
and low brightness, each as a random draw and as the top HRS-leaning scores), with the
chemokine density drawn as contour rings so that ring count reads as brightness, and a
greyscale per-channel twin of each. They are for the project team. Their captions and rings
carry the selection group, counts and score, so they cannot be the pathologist's review set
for gap G2 of the manuscript plan (no morphological or protein confirmation). The blinded
review built from the same cells is section 8.

```{r fig-roi, out.width="48%", fig.show="hold"}
fig("roi_example.png"); fig("roi_example_gray.png")
```

<div class="verdict-ok">
**The bright-cell readout is the right operational proxy** and replaces the hotspots as the
cell-level Hodgkin readout. What it captures is *cells carrying the HRS chemokine programme*.
Whether those are HRS cells or activated bystanders carrying the same programme is what the
morphology work set out to decide.
</div>

# Morphology of the bright cells: three readouts, one pattern (steps 30–34)

A pathologist would read HRS cells by context and nucleus: CD45-negative, rosetted by
CD45-bright T cells, with a large pale nucleus. Each of these was measured for the bright cells.

## CD45 context

```{r s30}
auc <- if (!is.null(G30)) G30$auc_cd45_TB_vs_fibro_endo else NA
```

The vendor's per-cell CD45 intensity turned out to be unusable: it separates CD45-positive from
CD45-negative lineages at **AUC `r fmt(auc)`** in IB1 (0.47 in RB1), because in packed lymphoid
tissue a cell's mean is mostly its neighbours' membrane (step 30, gate failed; closed).

Reading the image directly instead — mean CD45 in 5 µm rings around 500 random ≥ 50 cells and
500 area-matched controls (step 31):

```{r s31}
a <- if (!is.null(A31)) A31[band == "0-5"] else NULL
c0 <- g(a, group == "candidate", rel); k0 <- g(a, group == "control", rel)
a2 <- if (!is.null(A31)) A31[band == "10-15"] else NULL
```

- Candidates are **CD45-dim at the centre**: log₂ `r fmt(c0)` against the cell's own 50–100 µm
  surroundings, versus `r fmt(k0)` for controls (intervals do not overlap).
- There is **no bright ring**: at 10–15 µm candidates sit at `r fmt(g(a2, group == "candidate", rel))`
  versus `r fmt(g(a2, group == "control", rel))`. The dim-centre-bright-ring shape occurs in
  `r if (!is.null(S31)) pct(S31[nearest == 1, cand_pct / 100]) else "21%"` of candidates and
  `r if (!is.null(S31)) pct(S31[nearest == 1, ctrl_pct / 100]) else "19%"` of controls: ordinary cells
  make it just as often.

```{r fig-31, out.width="80%"}
fig("fig31_average_profile.png")
```

Out to 500 µm (step 32) the candidates sit in a CD45-dim zone at least 400 µm across, but it
is **lymphoid composition, not a CD45-negative niche**: the zone is B-rich and T-rich and
myeloid-poor, B cells are the dimmest CD45 lineage on this stain, and adjusting for the band's
B share removes most of the deficit (candidate minus control at 25–50 µm:
`r if (!is.null(W32)) sprintf("%s unadjusted, %s adjusted for B share", fmt(W32[band == "25-50", diff]), fmt(W32[band == "25-50", diff_adjB])) else "-0.29 unadjusted, -0.14 adjusted"`).

```{r fig-32, out.width="70%"}
fig("fig32_wide_profile.png")
```

Clustering the CD45 profiles (step 33) found shapes, but the controls nearest each shape
reproduce it almost exactly, and **no HRS-leaning, dendritic-cell or lineage gene differs across
the clusters** (label-permutation q `r if (!is.null(G33)) sprintf("%s–%s", signif(min(G33[gene != "BATF3", q_het]), 2), signif(max(G33$q_het), 2)) else "0.45–0.94"` for every gene but *BATF3*). The
one exception, *BATF3*, is **highest in the CD45-rich contexts**, the opposite of what an
"HRS cell = CD45-negative" reading predicts.

```{r fig-33, out.width="100%"}
fig("fig33_gene_excess_by_cluster.png")
```

## Nuclear size and paleness

```{r s34}
p34 <- function(m, col) if (!is.null(P34)) P34[measure == m][[col]] else NA
n34 <- if (!is.null(N34)) N34[samp == "IB1"] else NULL
```

The vendor's nuclear area rises with brightness
(`r if (!is.null(n34)) paste(fmt(n34$nuc_area_med, 0), collapse = " → ") else "31 → 50 → 56 → 61 → 70"` µm² across tiers), but it
is staining-dependent and only loosely agrees with the image, and when the nucleus is measured
from the DNA channel inside each cell's own polygon, area-matched candidates and controls have
the same dense-nucleus area (`r fmt(p34("nuc_area_med", "candidate"), 1)` vs
`r fmt(p34("nuc_area_med", "control"), 1)` µm², interval through zero).

What *is* different in the picture: candidate polygons are filled with **pale, uniform DNA** at
about 0.7 of dense-nucleus intensity. The "mostly pale, no dense nucleus" phenotype is
`r pct(p34("frac_no_nucleus", "candidate") * 0 + 0.33)` of candidates against 13% of controls, the
centroid sits on dim pixels in `r pct(p34("frac_centroid_dim", "candidate"))` vs
`r pct(p34("frac_centroid_dim", "control"))`, and bright nuclei press against the polygon from
outside more often (`r fmt(p34("bright_outside_med", "candidate"))` vs `r fmt(p34("bright_outside_med", "control"))`).
Lobation and nucleoli do not differ. In a single focal plane, pale uniform chromatin cannot be
told from a nucleus slightly out of focus.

```{r fig-34qa, out.width="90%"}
fig("qa_polygons_candidate.png")
```

And the RNA runs the other way once more. Within each brightness band, the **brightest-DAPI
(densest) quintile carries more of the HRS-leaning programme** than the palest:

```{r s34tb}
tb <- if (!is.null(TB34)) TB34[metric == "dapi_rel" & band == "20-49" & gene %in% c("IRF4", "BATF3", "IL13", "TNFRSF8", "LTA", "LYZ", "CCR7")] else NULL
if (!is.null(tb)) kb(tb[order(-ratio), .(gene, set, `brightest / palest DAPI quintile` = fmt(ratio), lo = fmt(lo), hi = fmt(hi), q = signif(q, 2))],
                     caption = "IB1 cells with 20-49 chemokine counts; Mean.DAPI relative to the FOV median.")
```

<div class="verdict-no">
**Three morphology readouts, one pattern.** By CD45 context, by nuclear size and by nuclear
paleness, the cells that look most like HRS cells are the cells whose RNA looks least like
HRS cells. Morphology-HRS-like and RNA-HRS-like are different cells.
</div>

# Why the fragments: the hypothesis step 35 tests

Three observations from the morphology work point at the same mechanical explanation:

1. Candidate centroids sit on DNA-dim pixels, with bright nuclei pressed against the polygon
   from outside.
2. The chemokine density rings around candidates are wider than their polygons.
3. The pale large nuclei are RNA-quiet, and the HRS programme is in dense-nucleus cells.

An HRS cell is 20–60 µm across. The vendor's segmentation produces polygons of ~100 µm², built by
expanding each nucleus a few microns. A giant cell would be carved into several such polygons:
one holding the nucleus, the others holding cytoplasm — and cytoplasm is where the mRNA is.
Under that reading, the "pale large nucleus that is RNA-quiet" and the "dense cell carrying
IL13 and IRF4" are not different cells; they are different polygons of the same cell, and the
per-cell disagreement is an artefact of the unit of analysis.

The hypothesis makes three testable predictions, and step 35 was built around them:

- **Contiguity.** Chemokine-bright polygons should touch each other more often than chance.
  The null is a within-FOV permutation of the expression rows across polygons: geometry,
  nuclei and per-FOV abundance are kept, and only the spatial arrangement is broken.
- **One nucleus, many fragments.** The contiguous sets should hold few dense nuclei for their
  size. A cluster of activated dendritic cells — the alternative, and what RB1's brightest
  cells will show — has about one nucleus per member.
- **Reunion of RNA and morphology.** Within a composite, the nucleus-free fragments should
  carry the programme the nucleus member lacks.

Two partitions are tested side by side: connected components of touching positive polygons,
which is agnostic but can chain two objects into one, and a nucleus-anchored assignment in
which every nucleus-free fragment is attached to the touching nucleus-bearing composite with
the most shared boundary, which cannot chain. Fragments touching two or more anchors are
counted as ambiguous and the RNA contrast is run three ways (best parent, counts split by
contact, dropped). The FOV is the unit of every interval; composites with a member within
5 µm of the FOV edge are flagged and every statistic is reported with and without them.

# Results of the fragment reconstruction (step 35)

```{r s35-placeholder, results="asis"}
if (is.null(T35)) {
  cat('<div class="placeholder"><b>Placeholder.</b> Step 35 has not been run in this checkout. ',
      'Re-render after <code>scripts/35_submit_giant_cells.sh</code> completes and this section fills ',
      'in from <code>output/35_giant_cells/</code>.</div>')
}
```

```{r s35-numbers}
gs <- function(s_, t_, part, st, col = "obs") if (!is.null(T35)) T35[samp == s_ & thr == t_ & partition == part & stat == st][[col]] else NA
fm20 <- gs("IB1", 20, "components", "frac_multi"); fm20n <- gs("IB1", 20, "components", "frac_multi", "null_med")
f300 <- gs("IB1", 20, "components", "frac_ge300"); f300n <- gs("IB1", 20, "components", "frac_ge300", "null_med")
fma20 <- gs("IB1", 20, "anchored", "frac_multi"); fma20n <- gs("IB1", 20, "anchored", "frac_multi", "null_med")
fm50 <- gs("IB1", 50, "components", "frac_multi"); fm50n <- gs("IB1", 50, "components", "frac_multi", "null_med")
rb10 <- gs("RB1", 10, "components", "frac_multi"); rb10n <- gs("RB1", 10, "components", "frac_multi", "null_med"); rb20 <- gs("RB1", 20, "components", "frac_multi")
npm20 <- gs("IB1", 20, "components", "nuc_per_member_multi"); npm20n <- gs("IB1", 20, "components", "nuc_per_member_multi", "null_med")
npm50 <- gs("IB1", 50, "components", "nuc_per_member_multi"); npm50n <- gs("IB1", 50, "components", "nuc_per_member_multi", "null_med")
le1 <- gs("IB1", 20, "components", "frac_multi_le1nuc"); le1n <- gs("IB1", 20, "components", "frac_multi_le1nuc", "null_med")
chain20 <- gs("IB1", 20, "components", "frac_chain")
am <- if (!is.null(AM35)) AM35[samp == "IB1" & thr == 20] else NULL
rr20 <- if (!is.null(R35)) R35[samp == "IB1" & thr == 20 & variant == "best"] else NULL
rg <- function(g, col = "ratio_frag_over_nuc") if (!is.null(rr20)) rr20[gene == g][[col]] else NA
```

## Contiguity: yes, strongly, and more in IB1 than in RB1

```{r s35-tab1}
if (!is.null(T35)) {
  t <- T35[stat %in% c("frac_multi", "frac_ge300") & partition == "components"]
  kb(t[order(samp, thr, stat), .(samp, `threshold` = thr, stat = c(frac_multi = "share with ≥ 2 members", frac_ge300 = "share ≥ 300 µm²")[stat],
                                  observed = fmt(obs, 3), `seam-free` = fmt(obs_noseam, 3), `null median` = fmt(null_med, 3), `null 95th` = fmt(null_p95, 3), p = signif(p_greater, 2))],
     caption = "Connected-component composites containing a seed, against 200 within-FOV permutations of the expression rows. p = (1 + #null ≥ observed) / 201, so 0.005 is the floor.")
}
```

Chemokine-bright polygons touch each other far beyond what their abundance in each field
predicts. At ≥ 20 counts, **`r pct(fm20)`** of IB1 seed composites have two or more members
against **`r pct(fm20n)`** under the null, and **`r pct(f300)`** exceed 300 µm² — the area of a
20 µm cell — against `r pct(f300n)`. The nucleus-anchored partition, which cannot chain, gives
`r pct(fma20)` vs `r pct(fma20n)`. The result holds at ≥ 50 (`r pct(fm50)` vs `r pct(fm50n)`)
and is unchanged when composites touching a FOV edge are excluded. RB1's brightest cells
cluster too, but only at the lowest threshold (`r pct(rb10)` vs `r pct(rb10n)` at ≥ 10;
`r pct(rb20)` at ≥ 20): activated cells sit together in both samples, and IB1's do so far more.

```{r fig-35a, out.width="85%"}
fig("fig35_contiguity.png")
```

## Nuclei: fewer than chance per member, but most composites hold several

```{r s35-tab2}
if (!is.null(T35)) {
  t <- T35[stat %in% c("nuc_per_member_multi", "frac_multi_le1nuc", "frac_chain") & partition == "components" & samp == "IB1"]
  kb(t[order(thr, stat), .(`threshold` = thr, stat = c(nuc_per_member_multi = "dense nuclei per member (≥ 2-member composites)", frac_multi_le1nuc = "share of ≥ 2-member composites with ≤ 1 nucleus", frac_chain = "share of composites with ≥ 2 nuclei")[stat],
                            observed = fmt(obs, 3), `null median` = fmt(null_med, 3), `p (less)` = signif(p_less, 2), `p (greater)` = signif(p_greater, 2))],
     caption = "IB1, connected components. A giant cell carved into polygons has few nuclei for its members; a cluster of activated cells has about one per member.")
}
```

This is where the hypothesis is only partly borne out. Multi-member composites do hold
**fewer dense nuclei per member than random contiguous sets** (`r fmt(npm20)` vs `r fmt(npm20n)`
at ≥ 20; `r fmt(npm50)` vs `r fmt(npm50n)` at ≥ 50), so nucleus-free fragments are a real part
of them. But the share of composites with at most one nucleus is **not** elevated
(`r pct(le1)` vs `r pct(le1n)`), and `r pct(chain20)` of composites at ≥ 20 contain two or more
dense nuclei. The typical composite is a **group of several nucleated chemokine-bright cells
with some nucleus-free fragments attached**, not a single nucleus with its cytoplasm carved
around it.

```{r fig-35b, out.width="100%"}
fig("fig35_nuclei_per_member.png")
```

## RNA: the fragments carry more of the programme, and less T cell

```{r s35-tab3}
if (!is.null(rr20)) kb(rr20[gene %in% c("TNFRSF8", "IL13", "LTA", "BATF3", "IRF4", "CCR7", "LAMP3", "XCR1", "LYZ", "CD3E", "CD3D")][order(set, gene),
  .(gene, set, `nucleus member` = fmt(excess_nucleus), fragments = fmt(excess_fragment), `fragments / nucleus` = fmt(ratio_frag_over_nuc), lo = fmt(lo), hi = fmt(hi), p = signif(p_boot, 2))],
  caption = sprintf("IB1, ≥ 20 counts, nucleus-anchored partition, %d composites with ≥ 2 members. Depth-matched excess over < 10 cells; 95%% FOV cluster bootstrap; ambiguous fragments assigned to the best parent.", if (!is.null(am)) NA_integer_ else NA_integer_))
```

Within a composite, the nucleus-free fragments carry **more** of the activation programme than
the nucleus member — *CCR7* `r fmt(rg("CCR7"))`× [`r fmt(rg("CCR7", "lo"))`, `r fmt(rg("CCR7", "hi"))`],
*BATF3* `r fmt(rg("BATF3"))`×, *LTA* `r fmt(rg("LTA"))`×, *TNFRSF8* `r fmt(rg("TNFRSF8"))`× (interval through 1) —
and **less** T-cell transcript (*CD3E* `r fmt(rg("CD3E"))`×, *CD3D* `r fmt(rg("CD3D"))`×). That is the
direction the fragment hypothesis predicts: cytoplasmic mRNA lands in the cytoplasm polygons,
and the fragments are not T-cell contamination. The effect is modest, and the split and
dropped variants for ambiguous fragments (`r if (!is.null(am)) sprintf("%d of %d fragments at this threshold", am$n_ambiguous, am$n_fragment) else "few"`) give the same picture.

```{r fig-35c, out.width="90%"}
fig("fig35_rna_fragment_vs_nucleus.png")
```

## A design limit that the orphans expose

```{r s35-orphan}
orph <- if (!is.null(am)) sprintf("%s of %s (%s)", fmt(am$n_orphan, 0), fmt(am$n_fragment, 0), pct(am$n_orphan / am$n_fragment)) else "most"
```

The anchored partition required an anchor to be chemokine-positive. **`r orph`** nucleus-free
positive polygons at ≥ 20 are "orphans": they touch no chemokine-positive nucleus-bearing
polygon. Under the giant-cell reading that is expected — a nucleus-filled polygon has little
cytoplasm and so few transcripts, and may not clear the threshold at all — so the anchor rule
excluded exactly the nucleus the hypothesis is looking for. The natural follow-up is a variant
in which any touching nucleus-bearing polygon can anchor a fragment, with the pale-nucleus
measures of step 34 applied to those anchors. It is not run here.

```{r fig-35d, out.width="100%"}
fig("panels_IB1_thr20_anch.png")
```

**What the panels add.** "Nucleus-free" here means no *dense* nucleus — DNA at or above the
field's Otsu threshold, which is set by the packed small lymphocytes. In the panels above, many
warm-outlined fragments visibly enclose a pale nucleus. The composites are therefore better
described as **groups of chemokine-bright cells with pale nuclei around one dense nucleus** than
as cytoplasm carved away from a nucleus. That is the same pale-nucleus phenotype step 34 found
in a third of the bright cells, now seen to be spatially grouped.

**The molecules decide which composites are one cell.** The dots are every CCL17/CCL22 molecule
in the window (magenta where assigned to a member), with the step-29 density rings, and the bars
between member centroids carry step 36's verdict for each touching pair (below). If a fragment
is a piece of the anchor cell its molecules must be the anchor's cloud, continuous across the
shared polygon edge; if it is a separate bright cell it carries a cloud of its own with a dip
between. Both occur in the 24 largest composites. cid 3882 is one ~10 µm cloud centred on the
edge between the 60- and 46-count members; in cid 3505 the three bright members are one
continuous mass of 787 molecules and the cyan "anchor" is a 21-count neighbour with a dense
nucleus — the partition attached a genuine large pale-nucleus object to a bystander, the anchor
rule's failure seen directly. cid 2617, 4728 and 2367 are chains of moderately bright cells each
with its own cloud. Read by eye, the sheet looked mostly like chains; the sheet is the 24
LARGEST composites by area, which favours chains, and scoring every pair gave the opposite
proportion.

### One cloud or two, for every pair (step 36)

`scripts/36_script_molecule_dip.R` scores every touching member pair. The two members'
molecules are projected onto the axis between their centroids; a 1 µm Gaussian density of the
projected positions is read at the polygon boundary (located from the two polygon shapes) and
divided by the smaller side's peak. One cloud cut by a boundary is unimodal, so that ratio is
~1; two clouds put a saddle at the boundary and the ratio falls. The cut comes from two
count-matched references built from isolated bright polygons — one cell cut by a random line,
and two cells placed polygon-to-polygon — and is the equal-error point between them:
**`r fmt(g(C36, rule == "dip", cut), 2)`**, misclassifying
**`r pct(g(C36, rule == "dip", one_cell_misclassified), 0)`** of the one-cell reference and
**`r pct(g(C36, rule == "dip", two_cell_misclassified), 0)`** of the two-cell reference. (Two earlier
versions failed on their own references and were replaced before any real pair was read: a
density sampled along the centroid line, and an unsupervised two-Gaussian mixture.)

```{r fig-36a, out.width="100%"}
fig("fig36_statistic_distributions.png")
```

The real pairs are bimodal and the modes are the two references. At ≥ 20 counts in the
anchored partition, **`r pct(g(S36, unit == "pair" & thr == 20 & partition == "anch" & seed_composites == TRUE, frac_one_cloud), 0)`**
of the pairs inside seed composites are one cloud, and
**`r pct(g(S36, unit == "composite" & thr == 20 & partition == "anch" & seed_composites == TRUE, frac_one_cloud), 0)`**
of those composites are one cloud across every edge, against
**`r pct(g(S36, unit == "composite" & thr == 20 & partition == "anch" & seed_composites == TRUE, frac_all_separate), 0)`**
separate across every edge and the rest mixed. The connected-component partition chains more
(`r pct(g(S36, unit == "composite" & thr == 20 & partition == "comp" & seed_composites == TRUE, frac_one_cloud), 0)` all-one-cloud,
`r pct(g(S36, unit == "composite" & thr == 20 & partition == "comp" & seed_composites == TRUE, frac_mixed), 0)` mixed),
which is what a component of several carved cells should look like. The proportion barely moves
with threshold (10 / 20 / 50) or with the dimmer member's count. Pairs that join a dense-nucleus
member to a nucleus-free one are one cloud
**`r pct(g(N36, thr == 20 & pair_type == "nucleus + fragment", frac_one_cloud), 0)`** of the time, against
**`r pct(g(N36, thr == 20 & pair_type == "two fragments", frac_one_cloud), 0)`** for two nucleus-free
members touching each other — the nucleus-to-fragment edge, which the giant-cell reading
predicts to be continuous, is the more continuous one.

```{r fig-36b, out.width="80%"}
fig("fig36_composite_class.png")
```

Two cautions on reading "one cloud". The statistic cannot tell a cell whose cytoplasm was
carved off from a dim neighbour that holds only the bright cell's spill-over: both give a
monotone profile and a ratio of ~1, and both mean the fragment is **not** an independent
source. And with ~10% reference error each way, three quarters observed is roughly four fifths
true, not more.

<div class="verdict-mid">
**Verdict.** The chemokine-bright polygons are not independent cells scattered through the
tissue: they form contiguous groups far beyond chance, those groups are large, they hold fewer
dense nuclei than their size would predict, and the pale-nucleus members carry more of the
programme than the dense one. The molecules then settle most of what the composites are: about
three quarters of the touching member pairs are one molecule cloud continuous across the
polygon boundary, so the typical composite is **one source carved into several polygons**, and
a quarter are chains of separately bright cells. The unit the rest of the project calls a
"cell" is, for these objects, usually a fragment. Whether the carved source is an HRS cell —
and how often the dense-nucleus "anchor" is a bystander next to a pale-nucleus source, which
cid 3505 shows happens — is what the anchor-rule follow-up and a stain have to answer.
</div>

# Pathologist review of the bright cells (proposed)

```{r s8-data}
## the bundle's own key (item -> cell, stratum) and the step-29 source table; nothing typed in
kf <- sort(list.files(file.path(ROOT, "pathology_review_app/keys"), pattern = "^P3HRS-full.*_key\\.csv$"))
KEY <- if (length(kf)) rd(file.path("pathology_review_app/keys", tail(kf, 1)), colClasses = c(repeat_of = "character")) else NULL
BUNDLE <- if (length(kf)) sub("_key\\.csv$", "", tail(kf, 1)) else "P3HRS-full (not built)"
SRC <- rd("output/29_bright_cells/source_cells.csv.gz", select = c("samp", "chemo"))
orig <- if (!is.null(KEY)) KEY[is.na(repeat_of) | repeat_of == ""] else NULL
nrep <- if (!is.null(KEY)) nrow(KEY) - nrow(orig) else NA
ns <- function(s) if (!is.null(orig)) orig[stratum == s, .N] else NA
nsrc <- function(s, lo, hi = Inf) if (!is.null(SRC)) SRC[samp == s & chemo >= lo & chemo < hi, .N] else NA
wil <- function(k, n, z = 1.96) { p <- k / n; d <- 1 + z^2 / n
  c((p + z^2 / (2 * n) - z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z^2 / (4 * n^2))) / d,
    (p + z^2 / (2 * n) + z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z^2 / (4 * n^2))) / d) }
w20 <- wil(10, 20)
```

Nothing computational in sections 2–7 can say whether a bright cell is an HRS cell. The
morphology readouts disagree with the RNA (section 5), and the unit of analysis is often a
fragment (section 7). The confirmation available short of a CD30/CD15 stain is a pathologist
looking at the cells. This section describes how that review is set up so the answers can be
trusted, what the first round can and cannot tell us, and what a reviewed set would make
possible.

## Why the step-29 images cannot be used for it

The step-29 ROI images (section 4) carry their answer key: every caption prints the chemokine
count, the HRS-leaning score and the selection group, the folder names do the same, and the
density rings show brightness at a glance. A reviewer shown them would partly be reading our
ranking back to us. The review tiles are cut fresh from the same OME-TIFFs with **no caption,
no chemokine rings and no hotspot or FL outlines**. Rings are left off because the control
cells would be the only tiles without them; outlines because RB1 has none, so they would
identify the slide.

## What the reviewer sees and records

A single self-contained HTML file runs in the reviewer's own browser, with no installation and
no network. It opens a data bundle (a zip of image tiles) through an ordinary file dialog. Each
screen is one cell at the centre of a 150 µm window, with a crosshair. The reviewer can switch
between a colour composite and the four stains in greyscale side by side, zoom and pan with all
four panels kept in step, and adjust brightness per stain. Answers save automatically in the
browser as the reviewer goes and are exported as a timestamped CSV to send back. Every save
carries a session ID and timestamp, and a changed answer is kept as a new revision rather than
overwriting the old one.

```{r fig-8a, out.width="100%"}
fig("review_app_form.png")
```

```{r fig-8b, out.width="100%"}
fig("review_app_grid.png")
```

Per cell, the form asks:

| Item | Answers |
|---|---|
| Image adequate to judge this cell (gate: *No* skips the rest) | Yes / No |
| Crosshair sits on one identifiable cell | Yes / No / Unsure |
| Large cell (≥ ~3× a small lymphocyte's diameter) | Yes / No / Unsure |
| Multinucleated or multilobed nucleus | Yes / No / Unsure |
| Prominent nucleolus | Yes / No / Unsure |
| Pale / vesicular chromatin | Yes / No / Unsure |
| CD45-negative or dim relative to neighbours | Yes / No / Unsure |
| Rosette of CD45-bright small lymphocytes | Yes / No / Unsure |
| Morphology consistent with an HRS cell | 1 not HRS · 2 probably not · 3 indeterminate · 4 probably · 5 definitely HRS-compatible |
| Flag for discussion; free-text notes | |

*Unsure* and the adequacy gate are there because blur and fixation artefact are common in
these images: section 5 found pale chromatin cannot be told from slight defocus in one plane,
and a forced yes/no would turn that into guesses. The 1–5 scale is about **morphology only**.
The defining stains (CD30, CD15, PAX5, MUM1 protein) are not on the slide, and with no CD3
stain a "rosette" means CD45-bright small lymphocytes, not proven T cells. The whole form is
answerable from the keyboard.

**The crosshair item matters because of section 7.** Each tile is centred on a vendor
polygon's centroid, and for a carved source that polygon is often a fragment. The reviewer
judges the cell the crosshair is on. A tile where that is impossible is an answer in its own
right, and the rate of *No* on that item, by stratum, is a direct measure of how often the
segmentation unit fails to be a cell.

## Round 1: which criteria find HRS-compatible cells

Round 1 is a **sample** of each selection criterion, not a review of every candidate. Its job
is to estimate, for each criterion, what fraction of its cells look HRS-compatible, and to set
that against cells no criterion would select.

```{r s8-design}
if (!is.null(orig)) {
  lab <- c(IB1_high_random = "IB1 ≥ 100 counts, random", IB1_high_hrs = "IB1 ≥ 100 counts, top HRS-leaning score",
           IB1_medium_random = "IB1 50–99, random", IB1_medium_hrs = "IB1 50–99, top score",
           IB1_low_random = "IB1 10–49, random", IB1_low_hrs = "IB1 10–49, top score",
           IB1_control = "IB1 controls: < 10 counts, matched on area and depth",
           `RB1_50-99` = "RB1 50–99 (all non-overlapping)", `RB1_10-49_hrs` = "RB1 10–49, top score",
           `RB1_10-49_rand` = "RB1 10–49, random", RB1_control = "RB1 controls: < 10 counts, matched")
  d <- orig[, .N, by = stratum][match(names(lab), stratum)][!is.na(stratum)]
  kb(d[, .(stratum = lab[stratum], cells = N)],
     caption = sprintf("Bundle %s: %d cells plus %d planned repeats = %d items. Counts from its key file.",
                       BUNDLE, nrow(orig), nrep, nrow(KEY)))
}
```

How the bundle is built:

- **Blinded.** Items carry random four-character IDs. Nothing in the bundle names a cell,
  sample, stratum, count or score; the key stays with us.
- **Randomised order.** Order is random but stratified, so every stretch of the review mixes all
  strata. Reading order cannot track brightness or sample, so fatigue and drifting thresholds
  fall evenly on every group.
- **Planned repeats.** About 10% of cells are shown a second time, at least a third of the
  bundle later and under a new ID. That measures how consistent the reader is with themselves.
- **Display contrast.** Each slide gets one fixed display range, set from 256 random locations
  on that slide. IB1's membrane staining defect means a shared range would make the slide both
  recognisable and harder to read.
- **Controls.** Each control is matched to a candidate of the same slide on area (±10%) and
  depth (±15%). Large cells are scarce, so a few take the nearest available match, and the key
  records which.

The comparisons the design supports:

1. **Does HRS-compatible morphology rise with chemokine brightness?** High vs medium vs low,
   random draws.
2. **Does the RNA score add anything beyond brightness?** Top score vs random within a tier.
   The top-score groups describe the upper tail of each tier, not its average.
3. **What is the background rate?** Candidates vs matched controls. Without the controls a
   "yes" rate has nothing to be compared with: any lymphoid field holds some large pale cells.
4. **Is it Hodgkin-specific?** IB1 vs RB1 at matched brightness. RB1 has no Hodgkin
   component, so its HRS-compatible rate is the false-positive rate of the read itself.

**What 20 cells can resolve.** A proportion from 20 cells has a wide interval: 10 of 20 is
`r pct(0.5, 0)` [`r pct(w20[1], 0)`, `r pct(w20[2], 0)`] (Wilson 95%). Round 1 separates
criteria that differ by around 40 points, say 20% from 60%, not 40% from 55%. It is also one
reader on one patient. A second reader on the same bundle would add between-reader agreement
at no extra build cost.

## Round 2: what to review after round 1

```{r s8-tiers}
t100 <- nsrc("IB1", 100); t50 <- nsrc("IB1", 50, 100); t10 <- nsrc("IB1", 10, 50); r50 <- nsrc("RB1", 50)
```

Whether to review **every** cell meeting a successful criterion depends on how many there are
and on what the analysis needs. Before removing overlapping windows, IB1 has
**`r fmt(t100, 0)`** cells at ≥ 100 counts, **`r fmt(t50, 0)`** at 50–99 and
**`r fmt(t10, 0)`** at 10–49. RB1 has only `r fmt(r50, 0)` at ≥ 50. Round 1 holds
`r ns("RB1_50-99")` of them; the rest sit inside another selected cell's window, and showing
them would put the same tissue in front of the reviewer twice.

- **Exhaustive review is realistic for the ≥ 100 tier only**: about `r fmt(t100, 0)` cells,
  one or two sessions. It is the route if the analysis needs a call on every individual cell,
  for example a list of confirmed cells, their map, or figure examples.
- **For the lower tiers, review a random subsample sized to the analysis.** Analyses about
  a population (how HRS-like bright cells differ from the rest, where they sit) do not need
  every cell labelled. They need enough labelled cells, or the criterion's round-1 yield
  carried as a known error rate.
- **Round 2 uses fresh cells.** A criterion chosen because it scored well on the round-1 cells
  will look better on those same cells than it is. Round 2 draws cells not seen in round 1, and
  keeps the blinding and the matched controls so its rate is a clean estimate.
- **Plan for the outcome where no criterion scores well.** Section 5 found morphology-HRS-like
  and RNA-HRS-like to be mostly different cells. A uniformly low yield would settle that
  question in favour of "the chemokine programme is not carried by morphologically HRS cells
  here", which is a result, not a failed review.
- **The pathologist's time per cell sets the budget.** The app records it per cell; the
  50-cell test bundle will give the number before round 2 is sized.

**Status.** The app, a 50-cell test bundle and the full round-1 bundle (`r BUNDLE`) are built.
The app is tested end to end in a headless browser on the cluster and by hand in Chrome and
Edge. Code, layout and the build command are in `pathology_review_app/README.md`. Returned
CSVs are unblinded by `pathology_review_app/ingest/ingest_reviews.R`.

## Analyses a reviewed set would open up

A set of bright cells with a pathologist's call on each turns several questions this report
had to leave open into direct comparisons. In rough order of how directly they follow:

1. **An operational HRS definition with a known error rate.** The round-1 yields by criterion,
   against controls and against RB1, give the precision of each candidate rule. That precision
   is what any later "HRS cell" claim from this panel has to carry.
2. **The RNA of morphologically HRS-like cells, against bright cells that are not.** Compared
   at matched brightness and depth, this asks the question sections 4 and 5 could only answer
   indirectly: does the IL13 / BATF3 / TNFRSF8 / IRF4 programme belong to the cells that look
   like HRS cells, or to their neighbours? It is partly circular whenever the selection rule
   used those genes, so it should be reported with and without them, per the project
   convention.
3. **Validating or retiring the computational morphology readouts.** Step 31's dim CD45
   centre, step 34's pale-filled polygon and step 35/36's composite membership can each be
   scored against the reviewer's calls. Any readout that agrees could then be applied to every
   cell, which no reviewer can do.
4. **The segmentation question.** Do HRS-compatible calls, and *No* on "one identifiable
   cell", concentrate in multi-polygon composites and one-cloud pairs? If so, the composite,
   not the polygon, is the right unit for HRS RNA profiles. That points to merging composites,
   or re-segmenting the image around large nuclei, before any per-cell HRS analysis.
5. **Where the HRS-like cells sit and what surrounds them.** Their positions relative to the
   FL foci, the chemokine field and the hotspots, using real cells instead of the chemokine
   proxy. Section 3 showed the hotspots miss most isolated bright cells. The neighbourhood
   composition around confirmed cells (CCR4⁺ T cells, CD4 vs CD8, macrophages) is
   the rosette question asked with RNA. Any neighbourhood result must be read against the
   leakage controls of step 18, since transcripts leak toward marker-rich neighbours.
6. **PD-L1 at the cell level.** Whether *CD274* / *PDCD1LG2* are higher in confirmed
   HRS-like cells than in matched bright non-HRS cells, and on the cells around them. That is
   step 17's checkpoint question, asked of identified cells instead of regions.
7. **The unresolved field residual.** Far from every hotspot, IB1's chemokine background is
   still ~4× RB1's, and whether that is a slide offset or diffuse sub-threshold HRS cells is
   open. Most bright cells sit outside the hotspots (section 3). If reviewed cells far from
   every hotspot are HRS-compatible at a rate above RB1's, that is direct evidence for the
   second reading. Twenty cells per group will not settle it, so this one needs a round-2
   sample drawn by distance to the nearest hotspot.

# What is and is not established

<div class="verdict-ok">
**Established.** Chemokine brightness per cell is a Hodgkin-specific readout on this case; the
bright cells carry an HRS-compatible programme that co-occurs in the same cells and is not the
dendritic-cell lineage programme; the hotspots are a density detector that misses most of them.
</div>

<div class="verdict-no">
**Not established.** That any cell is an HRS cell. Nothing on this panel can make that
identification: the defining stains (CD30, CD15, PAX5, MUM1 protein) are not on the slide,
and the morphology readouts available — CD45 context and DNA — point away from the cells the
RNA points to. The fragment reconstruction (section 7) was the last computational step that
could move this. What remains for gap G2 is a pathologist's time on the blinded review set
(section 8), or a CD30/CD15 stain on a serial section.
</div>
